node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Chance continuum
node.description: Place everyday chance words on a continuum from impossible through even chance to certain.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Even chance language
node.description: Use even chance or equally likely language when two outcomes or events are balanced in likelihood.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Context dependent likelihood
node.description: Judge chance language using contextual information rather than words alone.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Clear event criteria
node.description: Describe events with criteria clear enough that each outcome can be classified as occurring or not occurring.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Single outcome versus multiple-outcome event
node.description: Recognise that an event can contain one outcome or several favourable outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outcome recording consistency
node.description: Record chance experiment outcomes using consistent categories across repeated trials.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Frequency table for chance trials
node.description: Summarise repeated chance experiment outcomes in a frequency table.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Relative frequency introduction
node.description: Interpret the fraction or proportion of trials producing an outcome as its observed relative frequency.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Small-sample variability in chance experiments
node.description: Recognise that short runs of chance experiments can produce uneven or surprising results.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Long-run stability of relative frequency
node.description: Recognise that relative frequencies often become more stable as the number of trials increases.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Systematic outcome listing
node.description: Use a systematic order or structure to list all outcomes without omissions or duplicates.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample space completeness check
node.description: Check whether a sample space includes every possible outcome exactly once.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Table sample space for two-step chance situations
node.description: Use a table to organise outcomes for simple two-step chance situations.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outcome tree introduction
node.description: Use a simple branching diagram to organise outcomes in a sequential chance situation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Non-equally likely outcomes
node.description: Recognise chance situations where possible outcomes are not all equally likely.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Bias in chance devices
node.description: Recognise how unequal sections, repeated labels or physical bias can make chance devices unfair.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fair game outcome balance
node.description: Judge whether a simple game is fair by comparing the chances of each player winning.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Favourable outcomes in an event
node.description: Identify which outcomes in a sample space satisfy the event being considered.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Complementary event language
node.description: Describe the event that an outcome does not satisfy a given event as its complement in simple contexts.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Impossible event has no favourable outcomes
node.description: Connect impossible events to having no favourable outcomes in a sample space.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: More trials improve stability not certainty
node.description: Increasing the number of trials can make relative frequencies more stable but does not make the next outcome certain.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fair games give equal chances
node.description: A simple chance game is fair when players have equal chances of winning under the rules.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample space lists outcomes exactly once
node.description: A well-organised sample space includes each possible outcome once, without omissions or duplicates.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: An event may have multiple outcomes
node.description: An event can be satisfied by one outcome or by several outcomes in the sample space.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Impossible event has zero favourable outcomes
node.description: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes in the relevant sample space.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Observed outcomes are all possible outcomes
node.description: Learner lists only outcomes that occurred in trials and treats them as the complete sample space.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Small sample must match expected pattern
node.description: Learner expects a small number of trials to match the expected balance of outcomes exactly.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fair means everyone can win
node.description: Learner judges a game as fair merely because each player can win, rather than because the winning chances are equal.

edge.rationale: Ordering chance language directly practises comparing chance words.
Checking completeness directly practises sample-space construction.
Two-step tables are a common representation for organised sample spaces.
Summarising trial outcomes is a core part of conducting chance experiments.
Fair-game judgement directly practises fair/unfair chance situations.
Placing words on a chance continuum requires knowing everyday chance words first.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot order likely, unlikely, possible, impossible and certain consistently.

edge.rationale: Even chance is a more precise comparison within likely/unlikely language.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats even chance as very likely or impossible instead of balanced.

edge.rationale: Judging likelihood in context builds on ordering chance terms.
edge.failure_signal: Learner chooses chance words without considering the situation information.

edge.rationale: Event criteria require being able to decide whether an event can occur in a context.
edge.failure_signal: Learner describes events too vaguely to judge occurrence.

edge.rationale: Recognising event size builds on distinguishing outcomes from events.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes every event must be a single outcome.

edge.rationale: Consistent recording depends on recognising each trial and its outcome category.
edge.failure_signal: Learner mixes category definitions across repeated trials.

edge.rationale: A frequency table depends on recording trial outcomes consistently first.
edge.failure_signal: Learner tallies inconsistent outcome categories or double-counts trials.

edge.rationale: Relative frequency is calculated from counted trial frequencies and total trials.
edge.failure_signal: Learner reports counts but cannot compare them as proportions of trials.

edge.rationale: Small-sample variability is understood by comparing observed relative frequencies across trials or repetitions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner expects short-run results to match the long-run expected pattern exactly.

edge.rationale: Long-run stability contrasts with variability in small samples.
edge.failure_signal: Learner thinks more trials remove randomness entirely or guarantee exact alternation.

edge.rationale: Systematic listing builds on the goal of listing all possible outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner lists outcomes haphazardly and misses cases.

edge.rationale: Checking completeness depends on listing outcomes systematically.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot tell whether a sample space has omissions or duplicates.

edge.rationale: A two-step table is a specific organised sample-space representation.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot map first-step and second-step outcomes to table entries.

edge.rationale: Outcome trees are another organised representation for multi-step chance situations after tables.
edge.failure_signal: Learner omits branches or duplicates outcomes in a sequential diagram.

edge.rationale: Recognising non-equally likely cases builds on understanding equally likely outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes all possible outcomes have equal chance by default.

edge.rationale: Bias in chance devices is a cause of non-equally likely outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats uneven spinners or repeated labels as fair without checking outcome likelihoods.

edge.rationale: Judging fairness requires attending to balance or bias in the chance device and rules.
edge.failure_signal: Learner says a game is fair because everyone has a chance to win, even if chances differ.

edge.rationale: Identifying favourable outcomes requires knowing the relevant sample space.
edge.failure_signal: Learner counts outcomes outside the event or outside the sample space.

edge.rationale: Complement language contrasts outcomes that satisfy an event with those that do not.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot describe the non-event or counts it as overlapping the event.

edge.rationale: Connecting impossible events to zero favourable outcomes depends on identifying favourable outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats impossible as unlikely rather than no matching outcomes.
